stops.title: Why this paper
stops.text: Before we read SmolVLM, let me give you the few ideas it takes for granted. SmolVLM is a family of tiny models from Hugging Face that look at images and video and answer in text. The smallest has only 256 million parameters. For Assignment 1 that is good news, because a model this small is easy to fine-tune with LoRA on a free Colab or Kaggle GPU.

stops.title: Pictures become tokens
stops.text: First, a language model cannot see pixels. It only reads tokens. So the image is cut into small patches, a vision encoder called SigLIP turns them into over a thousand feature vectors, and a step called pixel shuffle folds neighbouring vectors together. A small projector then hands roughly sixty four visual tokens to the language model. Keep that pipeline in mind, because the whole paper is about making it cheaper.

stops.title: The token budget
stops.text: Why does the count matter so much? Because the context window, the number of tokens the model can read at once, is a fixed budget. The small SmolVLM models read about eight thousand tokens. Without compression, one detailed image nearly fills that, and a short video overflows it many times. With pixel shuffle, both fit easily.

stops.title: Words to know
stops.text: Glance at the glossary before you start. Three terms carry the paper: pixel shuffle, the context window, and SmolLM2, the small language model inside SmolVLM. You will also meet benchmark names like OCRBench, which tests reading text in images, and Video-MME, which tests video understanding. Come back here whenever a name stops you.

stops.title: Where it sits
stops.text: Finally, where does this paper sit? QLoRA gave you the fine-tuning tool, and TinyLLaVA Factory showed the standard recipe of vision encoder, projector and language model. SmolVLM shrinks that recipe and adds video, but it has no voice input, so you would pair it with a speech to text model. Voxtral, next, adds the voice path. When you're ready, press Play guided tour.
